plot.title: BCI communication rates over time
plot.observationBasis: Paper-reported · calculated · company · source-unverified approximate rate
plot.scope: 14 displayed observations: 9 PL R&D text-equivalent estimates included in the fit; 5 context marks excluded (2 paper-reported native task rates, 1 company native task rate and 2 approximate rates with unverified numerical sources).
plot.seriesNote:
Speech: PL R&D estimates use 1 assumed bit/character × five characters per word, including spaces (5 assumed bits/word). This context-dependent English-entropy model follows Stanford’s ‘Entropy and Redundancy in English,’ which describes estimates around 1 bit/letter. The selected weight and word-length factor are assumptions for these speech corpora. WPM × 5 × 1/60.

Handwriting and text selection/scanning use an equiprobable 28-symbol modeling alphabet: 26 letters, a space and one extra symbol are our declared choice, not the actual task keyboard. log2(28) ≈ 4.8 assumed bits/character is an ideal finite-codebook equivalent, not measured English entropy or 8-bit storage (a literal fixed-width 28-symbol code needs 5 bits). This normalization convention uses CPM × log2(28)/60 or log2(28)/seconds-per-letter. Calculations use full precision.

No extra WER/CER penalty: native correct-character rates already include correction time; the gross pace of speech and handwriting keeps reported errors separate. Vansteensel uses the reported 33 seconds/letter timing, not native correct CPM. Assistance and tasks differ: dictionary disambiguation, prediction, completion and language models can contribute to output. Correlations and language-model output mean these are not measured neural information rates, error-standardized results or a common performance benchmark.

The mixed-convention descriptive fit includes 9 text-equivalent observations; 5 context marks are excluded: 3 native task/company bits/s rates and 2 approximate rates with unverified numerical sources. Years indicate publication, preprint, journal issue or company disclosure; source dates are shown per observation. Bacher uses the 2015 issue (online 2014); Stentrode the 2021 issue (online 2020); home speech the 2025 preprint (final paper 2026). The 2015 cursor-control point has an unverified source and year.

points.label: Bacher et al.
points.sourceTitle: Reported input: Neural point-and-click communication by a person with incomplete locked-in syndrome
points.quote: In the “keyboard” task, the number of keystrokes per minute (QWERTY: 7.1 ± 1.7, Radial: 12.3 ± 1.1 kspm, p < 0.001) and the number of correct characters per minute (QWERTY: 5.7 ± 2.0, Radial: 9.4 ± 3.2 ccpm, p = 0.019) were higher using the Radial Keyboard compared to the QWERTY keyboard.
points.note: PL R&D estimate. Reported input: 9.4 ± 3.2 correct characters/minute; radial ‘keyboard ’ condition, completion off; ambiguous-key disambiguation retained (not the 10.4-CPM completion condition). 9.4 correct characters/minute × log2(28) bits/character ÷ 60. No extra error penalty: correct CPM already accounts for correction. Completion is off; ambiguous-key disambiguation remains. Publication/disclosure: 2014-11-10 (first online publication; 2015 journal issue).  Text-equivalent; fit included.

points.label: Synchron Stentrode
points.sourceTitle: Paper-reported estimate: Motor neuroprosthesis implanted with neurointerventional surgery improves capacity for activities of daily living tasks in severe paralysis
points.quote: The participant achieved 1.33 (1.58, 0.94–1.58) bits/trial at an ITR of 0.46 (0.41, 0.28–0.63) bits s -1 with the motor neuroprosthesis alone, and 4.43 (4.95, 3.85–4.95) bits/trial at an ITR of 1.57 (1.40, 0.98–2.11) bits s -1 was transmitted with the motor neuroprosthesis + eye-tracker.
points.note: Paper-reported estimate. Reported input: 0.46 bits/s, participant 2 mean estimated isolated motor-neuroprosthesis contribution.
